summary: Federated identity has mostly been used for network access and the web, with few common building blocks. This informational RFC describes the ABFAB architecture, which extends common security mechanisms so federated authentication can work for both web and non-web applications.

plainLanguage.summary: Federated sign-in lets a service ask an organisation the user already belongs to, instead of keeping its own user database. This document describes a way to do that for programs other than web browsers. It reuses the pieces that networks and applications already have, and rearranges them so the service never sees the user's long-term password.

questions: federated access beyond the web architecture
how does eap work in abfab
subtitle: How federated sign-in can work for protocols other than HTTP, by reusing the pieces networks already run.

tldr.problem: Federated access management has been built mostly for the web. Many non-web protocols have no native authentication framework, and new three-party authentication protocols are hard to build and even harder to deploy.
tldr.mechanism: ABFAB rearranges existing building blocks: RADIUS or Diameter between the relying party and the identity provider, EAP between the client and the identity provider, and a GSS-API mechanism that carries EAP to the application.
tldr.outcome: The result is an architecture that reaches many existing applications without changes, while the relying party never gets the client's long-term secret.

facts.label: Components of the IdP
facts.value: EAP server, RADIUS server, optional SAML service

today: RFC 7831 is an Informational document published in May 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it describes the architecture rather than a protocol on its own; the GSS-EAP mechanism it uses is specified in RFC 7055 and the SAML profile in RFC 7833.

sections.title: Why Federated Access Beyond the Web
sections.content:
Many security mechanisms have been deployed on the Internet to manage access to resources, and they have been generalized over the last decade through the Simple Authentication and Security Layer with GSS-API, the GS2 family, the Security Assertion Markup Language, and the Authentication, Authorization and Accounting architecture as embodied in RADIUS and Diameter.

A Relying Party (RP) is the entity that manages access to a resource. The entity requesting that access is often called the client. Some mechanisms let the RP delegate part of the access decision to an Identity Provider (IdP). That delegation needs technical signalling, trust and a common understanding of semantics between the RP and the IdP, and those aspects are managed inside a relationship known as a federation, so the style of access management is described as federated access management.

The document lists three benefits of federation. Single or simplified sign-on lets an Internet service delegate access management, and the associated responsibilities such as identity management and credentialing, to an organisation that already has a long-term relationship with the client. Data minimization and user participation cover the case where the RP does not need the client's identity but only certain attributes, such as an affiliation, a role or an entitlement, and sometimes only a pseudonym. Provisioning covers the case where the RP wants more, such as an email address or a name.

There are challenges too. As federations grow, the role of an Individual can become ambiguous: a school giving access to a student's grades to parents and to a teacher has to tell those roles apart on access. It also becomes harder to discover which IdP a user is associated with, and this is particularly acute for non-web systems, because many of them are not semantically rich enough to express such ambiguities. For example, SMTP and IMAP cannot ask the client for anything beyond the client NAI, which the server then uses to decide between the multiple federations it is associated with.

The stated design goals are that each party in a transaction is authenticated, though perhaps not identified, and the client is authorized for a specific resource; that the means of authentication is decoupled from the application protocol; that no long-term private keys are shared between clients and RPs; that the system scales to large numbers of IdPs, RPs and users; that it is designed primarily for non-web authentication; and that it builds on existing standards, components and operational practices. Designing new three-party authentication and authorization protocols is described as difficult and fraught with the risk of cryptographic flaws, and achieving widespread deployment is even more difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: Federation lets a service trust somebody else's answer about who the user is. That has mostly been built for web browsers. Many other protocols have no way to ask for a password at all, so this document works out how to reuse the network's own authentication machinery for them instead of inventing something new.

sections.title: The Entities and Their Relationships
sections.content:
Four entities appear in the model. The client is the entity asking for access. The IdP is the entity that vouches for the client. The RP is the entity that grants access to the resource. The Individual is a human being using the client; in any given situation an Individual may or may not exist, because clients can be front ends for Individuals or can be independent entities set up to run autonomously, such as the routers in the Trust Router Protocol, which use ABFAB to authenticate to each other.

The IdP and the RPs are part of a federation. The relationship may be direct, with an explicit trust relationship, or transitive, where the trust is mediated by one or more entities. A federation agreement typically encompasses operational specifications, which give enough definition for the system to work and for interoperability to be possible, and legal rules, which take the legal framework into consideration and set contractual obligations such as liability for losses, termination rights, enforcement mechanisms, measures of damage, dispute resolution and warranties.

The IdP typically has a long-term relationship with the client, involving the IdP identifying and credentialing the client, for example at the time of employment. The nature and quality of that relationship contribute to the level of trust an RP may assign to an assertion about a client, which is sometimes described as the level of assurance. Federation does not require a prior or long-term relationship between the RP and the client, and that property is what yields many of its benefits.

The document notes that the terminology sometimes appears inconsistent, because the standards it draws on use different words for the same concept. In this architecture the IdP consists of an EAP server, a RADIUS server and, optionally, a SAML Assertion service. The document uses the term Network Access Identifier (NAI) as defined in RFC 7542: an NAI consists of a realm identifier, which is associated with an AAA server and thus an IdP, and a username associated with a specific client of that IdP.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things are involved: the client that wants access, the service it wants, the organisation that vouches for the client, and the human being behind the client if there is one. The service and the vouching organisation are tied together by an agreement that covers both the technical details and the legal rules.

sections.title: How the Authentication Runs
sections.content:
The architecture reuses existing building blocks and rearranges them. The protocol that carries the authentication between client and service is GSS-API, chosen for ease of integration with a wide range of non-web application protocols; the technical specification of the GSS-EAP mechanism is in RFC 7055. Between the service and the identity provider the architecture uses the AAA framework, and the main body of the document describes shared secret authentication, which is the easiest to implement.

The described run has twelve steps. The client is configured with an NAI assigned by the IdP and with the secrets needed to run EAP between it and the IdP, and it is configured to use the GSS-EAP GSS-API mechanism. The client sets up a transport to the RP and begins GSS-EAP authentication; the RP replies with an EAP request asking for the client's name, and the client answers with an EAP response whose NAI name form contains at least the realm portion of its full NAI.

The RP then uses preconfigured information or a federation proxy to work out which IdP to use, based on policy and the realm portion of the NAI. Once it knows the IdP, the RP or its agent sends a RADIUS request, whose Access-Request encapsulates the EAP response. At this stage the RP has no idea who the client is; it sends its own identity to the IdP in AAA attributes and may send a SAML request in an AAA attribute, and the AAA network checks that the identity claimed by the RP is valid.

The IdP sends an EAP message to the client naming the method to be used. It should not re-request the client's name in this message, but clients need to be able to handle it, and the IdP must accept a realm only, in order to protect the client's name from the RP. A number of EAP messages then pass between the client and the IdP until the result of the authentication protocol is determined. As part of the method the client sends an EAP channel-binding message to the IdP, identifying among other things the RP to which it is attempting to authenticate; the IdP checks that channel-binding data against the data the RP supplied over AAA, and sends an EAP failure if the bindings do not match.

Once EAP succeeds, the client and the IdP hold two keys, a Master Session Key and an Extended MSK. The IdP then applies local policy to decide whether the RP and client are authorized for the transaction, and which attributes, if any, will be released to the RP. If the IdP sends a success result to the RP, it may also send AAA attributes about the client, usually as one or more SAML Assertions, and it returns the EAP MSK to the RP. The RP then has enough information to grant or refuse access, and it returns the result to the client. The client can now complete the authentication of the RP by using the EAP MSK value.
sections.plainLanguage: The run has three legs. The client talks to the service and says which organisation it belongs to. The service passes that on to the organisation, which runs the actual authentication exchange with the client. When that succeeds the organisation sends the service a session key and, if the policy allows, some details about the user, and the service passes the result back to the client.

sections.title: The Protocols That Carry Each Leg
sections.content:
Communication between the RP and the IdP is done by the Federation Substrate, which is responsible for establishing the trust relationship, determining the rules that govern the relationship, conveying authentication packets from the client to the IdP and back, providing the means of establishing a trust relationship between the RP and the client, and giving the RP a way to obtain attributes about the client. The ABFAB working group chose the AAA framework for those messages. In AAA terms the IdP is the AAA server, the RP is the AAA client, and the building blocks of a federation are AAA proxies, relays and redirect agents. RADIUS is often found in enterprise and university networks and with fixed network operators, while Diameter is deployed by mobile network operators; the document defines all the new AAA attributes as RADIUS attributes and leaves the choice to implementers.

Between the client and the IdP the architecture uses EAP, which is an end-to-end framework providing two-way communication between a peer, through the EAP authenticator, to the back end. One requirement is that the RP must not get possession of the long-term secret of the client, both because a valuable secret would be exposed and because a synchronization problem can develop when the client changes keys with the IdP. The framework must also allow different authentication mechanisms to be integrated, since some IdPs require hardware tokens while others use passwords. The EAP method used must provide mutual authentication of the client and IdP and support channel binding; as of writing, the only method meeting both criteria is TEAP, either alone when client certificates are used or with an inner EAP method that does mutual authentication.

Between the client and the RP the architecture uses GSS-API, which many applications such as SSH, NFS and DNS already support, together with SASL, which IMAP, SMTP, XMPP and LDAP support. Using a GSS-API mechanism with SASL requires placing some headers before the mechanism's messages and constraining certain GSS-API options. GSS-API creates and consumes messages but does not provide the transport, so the application protocol must do that; the transport does not need to provide confidentiality or integrity, but it must be reliable, must deliver tokens in order during negotiation, and must deliver GSS-API messages atomically.

Two different facilities are called channel binding. EAP channel binding sends attributes from the peer to the EAP server, either as part of the EAP conversation or as part of a secure association protocol, and the EAP server confirms the consistency of these attributes and provides the confirmation back to the peer. GSS-API channel binding protects against man-in-the-middle attacks when GSS-API is used inside a tunnel, and works by each side deriving a cryptographic value from the tunnel and using it to prove to the other side that it knows the value. GSS-API channel binding specifies that there is nobody between the client and the EAP authenticator, while EAP channel binding allows the client to have knowledge of authenticator attributes such as the authenticator's name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each leg of the exchange uses machinery that already exists. The network protocol between the service and the organisation is RADIUS or Diameter. The conversation with the user is EAP, run inside a GSS-API mechanism that the application already knows about. The point of the arrangement is that the service never holds the user's long-term secret.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The document groups the entities into three phases and names the observers in each. In the client-to-RP phase the client is the initiator and the RP the recipient. In the client-to-IdP phase, which runs through the Federation Substrate, the observers are the client, the RP, the AAA client, the AAA proxies and the AAA server, and the IdP. In the IdP-to-RP phase the RP is the initiator and the observers are the IdP, the AAA server, the proxies, the AAA client and the RP. Eavesdroppers and attackers can reside on any or all of the links. Entities may also collude: if an RP and an AAA proxy collude, the trust of the system is broken, because the RP could lie about its own identity to the IdP, and the document says there is no known way to deal with that.

In the initial phase the client sends an NAI to the RP, and many EAP methods allow the client to disclose it with only a realm component, which is the minimum needed to indicate an IdP the principal has a relationship with. Methods that do not allow this necessarily reveal an identifier such as a username.

In the client-to-IdP phase the EAP MSK is transported between the IdP and the RP over the AAA infrastructure. This is a particularly important privacy consideration, because any AAA proxy that has access to the MSK can decrypt and eavesdrop on any traffic encrypted with it, which is all traffic between the client and the RP. The AAA server has the material needed to derive the session key, so it can observe that traffic too; the document notes that this was chosen as a simplification and to make performance faster, and that extensions using Diffie-Hellman key exchange would mitigate it.

In the IdP-to-RP phase the IdP may send explicit identity information about the principal, through RADIUS headers or using SAML, and what is released is controlled by policy on the IdP. When it is sent using SAML as specified in RFC 7833, confidentiality should be guaranteed, because that specification requires TLS for RADIUS.

On the relationship between user and entities, the document notes that in cases where RPs do not need to identify a particular Individual, the architecture enables anonymous or pseudonymous access, so data and identifiers other than pseudonyms and unlinkable attribute information need not be stored. Where an RP does need to identify a person, that information has to be collected, stored and retained for as long as it is required, and for privacy protection it should be deleted when it is no longer needed. The document also notes that users are active participants in initiating the exchange, but they are not involved in controlling the information transmitted from the IdP to the RP; with the current ABFAB flows there is no place for a process of gaining user consent for that release.
sections.plainLanguage: More parties see more of what is exchanged, and the document names them. The network's own proxies carry the session key that protects the conversation between the user and the service, so they can read it. And the user cannot say which details about them the organisation is allowed to pass on; that is decided by the organisation's policy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security is the main focus of the architecture, and the document points back to the privacy section. TLS appears in many places in the design. While anonymous connections can be used in some places, such as between the client and the RP, it is important that TLS connections within the AAA infrastructure and between the client and the IdP be fully authenticated, and that certificate revocation be checked as well. With anonymous connections between client and RP, all messages and data exchanged between those two are visible to an active attacker. Clients also need the trust anchor for the IdP configured correctly, which is a difficult problem in general and harder still in kiosk environments.

The choice of EAP methods matters. A tunnelling method such as TEAP allows other EAP methods to be used while hiding the contents of those exchanges from the RP and from the AAA framework, and the considerations about binding inner and outer EAP methods apply. Where SAML statements are used, RPs will generally be unable to validate signatures on the SAML statement, either because the IdP stripped the signature or because the RP cannot validate the binding between signer, key and realm, so it is required that IdPs do the trust checking and that RPs can trust the AAA infrastructure to keep the statements valid.

Finally, when a pseudonym is generated as a unique long-term identifier for a client by an IdP, care must be taken that the algorithm cannot be easily reverse-engineered by the service provider. If it can be, the provider can consult an oracle to find out whether a given long-term identifier belongs to a different known identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The protection of the whole scheme depends on the tunnels between the pieces being properly secured, especially the ones inside the network. It also depends on the choice of authentication method, on the organisation checking the signatures it sends, and on the pseudonyms it hands out not being reversible.

messages.label: EAP request for the name
messages.note: Sent inside GSS-EAP when the client starts authentication with the RP.

messages.label: EAP response with the NAI realm
messages.note: At minimum the realm, which names the IdP the client has a relationship with.

messages.label: RADIUS Access-Request
messages.note: Carries the EAP response and the RP's own identity in AAA attributes.

messages.label: EAP method to use
messages.note: Travelled through the RP and the AAA infrastructure.

messages.label: EAP exchange with the method
messages.note: How many messages this takes depends on the method chosen.

messages.label: EAP channel binding
messages.note: Names the RP, so the IdP can check it against what the RP said.

messages.label: Access-Accept with the MSK
messages.note: The EAP MSK, plus attributes such as SAML Assertions if policy allows.

messages.label: Result of the authentication
messages.note: The client can then check the identity of the RP using the MSK.

viz.caption: WHAT THE PRIVACY SECTION POINTS OUT (RFC 7831, SECTION 4)

items.title: The service can see the client's address
items.text: The RP knows the client's IP address and could put it in a RADIUS header.

items.title: Proxies on the path can read everything
items.text: AAA gives no end-to-end protection, so every entity on the path can eavesdrop.

items.title: The session key travels over AAA
items.text: Any proxy with the EAP MSK can decrypt the traffic between the client and the RP.

items.title: The AAA server holds the session key
items.text: It can observe the client-to-RP traffic, a simplification chosen for speed.

items.title: A colluding service and proxy break trust
items.text: The service could lie about its own identity, and the document says there is no known fix.

items.title: Users do not consent to releases
items.text: What the IdP passes to the RP is set by IdP policy, with no place for consent in the flows.
